content_voiceover: Two more classification-heavy questions. Question one asks which mutation is not high risk under MIPSS seventy version two for primary myelofibrosis. The high molecular risk category includes ASXL1, SRSF2, EZH2, and IDH1 or IDH2 mutations, each carrying prognostic weight in the calculator. DNMT3A, despite being one of the most common myeloid mutations overall, is not counted among these high-risk drivers, so it's the correct answer. Question two tests the fifth edition WHO and ICC criteria for Philadelphia-negative MPNs, which stayed largely similar to the fourth edition. The wrong statement here is option C, because it borrows features that actually define prefibrotic early myelofibrosis, things like increased age-adjusted marrow cellularity, granulocytic proliferation, and reduced erythropoiesis, and misattributes them to true essential thrombocythemia. True ET marrow should not show those proliferative, hypercellular changes; that distinction between ET and prePMF is exactly what the morphologic criteria are designed to catch.
keypoints: MIPSS70v2 high-risk mutations: ASXL1, SRSF2, EZH2, IDH1/2 (not DNMT3A)
5th WHO/ICC MPN criteria largely mirror the 4th edition
True ET marrow lacks hypercellularity, granulocytic proliferation, or decreased erythropoiesis
Those proliferative features actually define prefibrotic early myelofibrosis
keypoint_voiceover: Remember the MIPSS seventy version two high molecular risk set, ASXL1, SRSF2, EZH2, and IDH1 or IDH2, while DNMT3A sits outside that high-risk group. And when you see hypercellular marrow with granulocytic proliferation and reduced erythropoiesis attributed to essential thrombocythemia, recognize that as prefibrotic early myelofibrosis instead, since true ET marrow stays comparatively bland.
